claims.claim: Jupiter is the biggest planet in the solar system.
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/ (Planetary Fact Sheet, Mass and Diameter rows)
claims.note: Jupiter has the largest mass (1898e24 kg) and diameter (142,984 km) of the eight planets. Hook (A4): a viewer who swipes after this sentence leaves with a true fact.

claims.claim: Two and a half times the mass of every other planet combined.
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/ and the per-planet sheets (mercury/venus/earth/mars/saturn/uranus/neptune/jupiterfact.html), Mass row

claims.claim: JUPITER / 2.5× the other planets / combined, by mass
claims.source_checked: Same NASA fact sheets as claim 2

claims.claim: Row of the other seven planets beside Jupiter at one scale: Saturn 0.833, Uranus 0.363, Neptune 0.352, Earth 0.091, Venus 0.087, Mars 0.0485, Mercury 0.035 of Jupiter's radius
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/<planet>fact.html, Volumetric mean radius row for each planet
claims.note: Volumetric mean radii over Jupiter's 69,911 km: Saturn 58,232 (0.833), Uranus 25,362 (0.363), Neptune 24,622 (0.352), Earth 6,371 (0.0911), Venus 6,051.8 (0.0866), Mars 3,389.5 (0.0485), Mercury 2,439.7 (0.0349). All drawn values match to the stated precision.

claims.claim: But hold Jupiter up next to the Sun, and it looks tiny. (Jupiter drawn at radius 52 beside the Sun at 520)
claims.where: spoken + on-screen: Jupiter beside the Sun
claims.note: 695,700 / 69,911 = 9.95; drawn ratio 520/52 = 10.0. 'Looks tiny' is fair at about a tenth of the width.

claims.claim: It would take nearly a thousand Jupiters to fill the Sun.
claims.note: Volume ratio 986.5, so 'nearly a thousand' is accurate and does not overshoot. It is a volume equivalence (solid spheres could not fill it); the on-screen sub says 'by volume', which carries that.

claims.claim: ≈ 1,000 JUPITERS / to fill it, by volume / dots not to scale (1,000 small dots spread across the Sun's disc)
claims.source_checked: Same NASA Sun and Jupiter fact sheets as claim 6
claims.note: 986.5 shown as ≈ 1,000; 'by volume' and 'dots not to scale' are on screen, so the non-to-scale dots are disclosed (A6).

claims.claim: Our Sun is not an average star. It is an unusually big one.
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021, A&A 650, A201, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985, arXiv:2104.14972 LaTeX source, Table 3 (tab:numbers) and Sect. on spectral types; Boyajian et al. 2012 arXiv:1208.2431 Table 6
claims.note: Within 10 pc the Sun is larger than at least 90.8% of typed stars (see claim 9), so it is above the typical (median) star and in the top ~9%.

claims.claim: It is bigger and brighter than over ninety percent of the stars in our part of the galaxy
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021 (arXiv:2104.14972 source) Table 3: A 4, F 8, G 18, K 38, M 249, D 20, N/A 41, Sun excluded; text: the 41 untyped are all close-binary secondaries, estimated as 36 possible M, 4 possible L, 1 possible WD; M types are classed as low-mass stars. Boyajian et al. 2012 (arXiv:1208.2431, doi:10.1088/0004-637X/757/2/112) Table 6 'Fundamental Parameters': largest GJ 702A K0 Ve 0.8310 R_sun, 0.53 L_sun; GJ 75 0.819, 0.52; GJ 166A 0.806, 0.408; all M dwarfs <= 0.5773 R_sun and 0.0697 L_sun. Giammichele et al. 2012 (arXiv:1202.5581, doi:10.1088/0067-0049/199/2/29) Table 2, all 165 rows parsed: brightest log L = -1.12 (WD 1620-391), brightest within 10 pc Sirius B (0642-166) log L = -1.53, max Stefan-Boltzmann radius 0.0216 R_sun. Thévenin et al. 2005 (astro-ph/0501420, doi:10.1051/0004-6361:20042075) Table 1: delta Eri D/D_sun = 2.33 +/- 0.03, L = 3.19 L_sun.
claims.note: Worst case (all A, F, G stars plus delta Eri counted as bigger, untyped excluded): 306/337 = 90.8%. Including the 37 untyped objects Reylé estimates to be stars: 343/374 = 91.7%. Brown dwarfs among the M types would need to exceed ~27 to push this under 90%. Limit of this check: the per-star luminosity classes in Reylé Table A.1 (CDS J/A+A/650/A201) could not be reached (CDS blocked), so 'delta Eri is the only K star larger than the Sun' was not verified star by star; the claim survives even if 3 more K stars were larger. 'Our part of the galaxy' matches the paper's scope (keyword 'Galaxy: solar neighbourhood', 10 pc census).

claims.claim: THE SUN / bigger than 9 in 10 nearby stars
claims.note: Worst-case 90.8% >= 9 in 10; 'nearby' matches the 10 pc census.

claims.claim: because most of them are red dwarfs: small, dim, and everywhere.
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021 Table 3 and text ('We found 249 M stars among the 423 objects with a measured spectral type ... 58.9 +/- 5.8%'; abstract: 'around 61% are M stars'); Boyajian et al. 2012 Table 6 (M dwarfs 0.141-0.577 R_sun, 0.00155-0.0697 L_sun)
claims.note: M dwarfs are 249/337 = 74% of typed stars, 58.9% of all typed objects including brown dwarfs: a majority under every reading. The 'because' names the main reason; K dwarfs and white dwarfs supply the rest of the >90%, which is an acceptable simplification, not a false cause.

claims.claim: 10×10 grid of 100 dots: 8 large bright yellow (G or hotter), 10 orange (K), 5 tiny white (white dwarfs), 77 red (M or untyped); 'dots: star type, not size'
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021 Table 3 and the paragraph on the 41 untyped objects (arXiv:2104.14972 source)
claims.note: Per 100 of 379 (337 typed + 41 untyped + Sun): 31 -> 8.2, 38 -> 10.0, 20 -> 5.3, 290 -> 76.5, giving 8/10/5/77. Using Reylé's own estimates for the untyped (36 M, 4 L brown dwarfs, 1 WD) and dropping the 4 brown dwarfs gives 8/10/6/76 of 375; the difference is one dot and does not change the picture. Optional tidy-up: SOURCES claim 9 says only '36 of which Reylé lists as possible M dwarfs'; it could add that the other 5 are 4 possible L dwarfs and 1 possible white dwarf. Dot sizes differ by class but the screen says 'not size' (A6).

claims.claim: So look at the nearest star to our own. Proxima Centauri ... The closest star to the Sun
claims.source_checked: Anglada-Escudé et al. 2016, Nature 536, 437, doi:10.1038/nature19106, arXiv:1609.03449 source: 'At a distance of 1.295 parsecs, the red-dwarf Proxima Centauri ... is the Sun's closest stellar neighbour'
claims.note: Wording matches the source; 'closest star to the Sun' correctly avoids 'closest star to us'.

claims.claim: just over four light years away.
claims.source_checked: NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP, pscomppars, Proxima Cen b/d: sy_dist 1.30119 (+0.00034/-0.00035) pc (ref TICv8, Stassun et al. 2019)
claims.note: 1.30119 pc x 3.2616 = 4.244 ly; Anglada-Escudé's 1.295 pc = 4.22 ly. 'Just over four' holds for both.

claims.claim: PROXIMA CENTAURI / ≈ 1/7 the Sun's radius (drawn 13.7 against the Sun's 96)
claims.source_checked: Kervella et al. 2017, A&A 598, L7, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/201629930, arXiv:1611.03495 source (macros RProx = 0.141 +/- 0.007 interferometric, Demory et al. 2009; RProxMann = 0.1542 +/- 0.0045 from the radius-M_Ks relation); Anglada-Escudé 2016 ('measured radius of 0.14 R_sun'; table 0.141 [0.120,0.162]); Boyajian 2012 Table 6 GJ 551 0.1410 +/- 0.0070; NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars st_rad 0.141 +/- 0.021 (Suárez Mascareño et al. 2025, 2025A&A...700A..11M)
claims.note: 1/7 = 0.143 and the drawing 13.7/96 = 0.143 sit inside the measured 0.141 +/- 0.007 and the Archive range; the model value 0.154 (~1/6.5) is recorded in SOURCES as the disagreement, and '≈' covers it. Proxima drawn as a red dot matches its M5.5 V type (Archive st_spectype).

claims.claim: and you have almost certainly never seen it. It is almost always too faint for your eyes.
claims.source_checked: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars sy_vmag 11.01 (TICv8); Howard et al. 2018, ApJL 860, L30, doi:10.3847/2041-8213/aacaf3, arXiv:1804.02001 source
claims.note: V = 11.0 is about 60x fainter than a ~6.5 mag naked-eye limit. Howard: 'no M-dwarfs are usually visible to the naked-eye'; the March 2016 superflare (~68x) made Proxima 'briefly ... a g'=6.8 star, at the limit of visibility to trained observers at very dark sites'. Both 'almost' hedges are supported.

claims.claim: That is what most of the stars around us look like. (the 8 bright dots fade out)
claims.source_checked: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars st_spectype 'M5.5 V' (Suárez Mascareño et al. 2025); Reylé et al. 2021 Table 3
claims.note: Proxima is an M dwarf, and M dwarfs are 74% of typed stars within 10 pc (58.9% of all typed objects including brown dwarfs), so 'most' holds. Fading the G-and-hotter dots leaves 92 of 100, consistent.

claims.claim: The star we call ordinary is one of the rare big ones. (the Sun returns into the grid as one of the 8; 'THE SUN / one of the few')
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021 Table 3; Boyajian et al. 2012 Table 6; Giammichele et al. 2012 Table 2; Thévenin et al. 2005
claims.note: A 4 + F 8 + G 18 + Sun = 31 of 379 (8%). Because the Sun is larger than at least 90.8% of typed stars (claim 9), it is in the top ~9% by size, so 'one of the rare big ones' / 'one of the few' holds whether or not the smaller late-G stars are counted in that group.
